records.sourceFile: Supplement use in patients undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Greif DN, Emerson CP, Allegra P, Arizpe A, Mansour KL, Cade WH II, et al. Supplement Use in Patients Undergoing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review. Arthroscopy: The Journal of Arthroscopic and Related Surgery. 2020.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA systematic review asked whether a standardized dietary supplement can reduce post-operative muscle atrophy or improve rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction. Ten randomized trials were included, and protein or amino acid supplementation was the only type with potentially beneficial results.
paper.tldr: Protein or amino acid supplements showed the most promising results for muscle recovery after ACL reconstruction, but the trials are small and of low quality. No specific protein protocol can be recommended, and creatine, vitamin C and E, and testosterone did not show benefit.
paper.methods: Two reviewers searched MEDLINE, Scopus and the Cochrane Library in July 2019 following PRISMA. Only English-language randomized controlled trials of protein, amino acid, vitamin, hormone or other supplements in ACL reconstruction were included, and risk of bias was rated with the Cochrane tool.
paper.findings: Among four protein or amino acid trials (177 patients), two reported significant advantages over placebo in isokinetic strength or in the number of rehabilitation sessions needed to reach benchmarks, two reported greater thigh hypertrophy, and one (Vidriero et al.) reported improved IKDC scores and less analgesic use; Holm et al.'s muscle biopsies showed no difference and the glucosamine trial found no benefit. One creatine trial (60 patients) found no between-group differences. Vitamin C and E trials found no benefit on serum cytokines or strength, peak isometric force was greater with placebo at three months, and biopsies showed more inflammatory cell infiltration in the vitamin group. One testosterone trial in six men found greater total lean mass at six weeks only, with no difference in injured-leg strength or clinical scores at any time point.
paper.limitations: The review is limited by the small number of eligible trials, heterogeneity in supplements, doses, timing and outcomes, and a low overall quality of evidence. The population is ACL reconstruction patients rather than athletes in general, and the authors state the findings cannot be generalized to other knee sports procedures. Only one group's cohort was used across three vitamin trials, and the protein trial by Eraslan and Ulkar started supplements six weeks after surgery.
paper.practicalImplications: Protein or amino acid supplementation may be considered as an adjunct to ACL rehabilitation, but this review does not identify a dose, timing or product. Creatine, vitamin C and E, and testosterone should not be expected to reduce post-operative atrophy on current evidence.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the trials enrolled ACL reconstruction patients rather than healthy athletes, so they cannot set a performance supplement protocol. The protein findings concern regaining quadriceps size and strength after surgery.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the protein trials report faster rehabilitation benchmark achievement and some strength gains, which may inform rehab planning. The review does not show that any supplement shortens time to return to sport or lowers re-injury risk, so it cannot support a return-to-play decision.

records.sourceFile: Sweat characteristics of cramp-prone and cramp-resistant athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Miller KC, McDermott BP, Yeargin SW. Sweat Characteristics of Cramp-Prone and Cramp-Resistant Athletes. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2020 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This multicenter cross-sectional study compared sweat rates and sweat electrolyte concentrations and content in 350 collegiate athletes with and without a history of exercise-associated muscle cramps. Within each sex, the groups did not differ, and sweat variables predicted cramp history only in American football.
paper.tldr: Sweat rate and sweat electrolyte losses did not differ between college athletes with and without a cramp history in most sports, so fluid and electrolyte losses alone do not appear to explain cramps for most athletes. Heavy sweaters in American football may warrant individual hydration and electrolyte monitoring.
paper.methods: Division I athletes from 11 sports completed one habitual practice or conditioning session. Sweat rate was calculated from pre- and post-exercise body mass corrected for fluid intake, and posterior forearm sweat patches were analysed for sodium, potassium and chloride. Crampers and non-crampers were compared by sex with two-way ANOVA, and ROC analysis with cut points tested which sweat variables predicted cramp history, with P < .01 as the significance threshold.
paper.findings: Within each sex, no differences in sweat rate or sweat sodium, potassium or chloride concentration or content were found between crampers and non-crampers; female potassium content showed P = .03, which did not meet the study's P < .01 threshold. In American football, sweat rate and sodium, potassium and chloride content predicted cramp history (AUC 0.65-0.72, P <= .005); the authors also report that a sweat rate per body surface area above 0.75 L per hour per m2 carried about six times the odds of being cramp-prone, although that variable's AUC (0.62, P = .02) did not reach significance. With American football removed, no sweat variable predicted cramp history, and males lost more sweat and electrolytes than females.
paper.limitations: Cramp history was self-reported, and the authors did not separate local from whole-body cramps. Field conditions could not control hydration status, fluid type or duration, and sweat patches collected primary sweat that may overstate concentrations. No athlete cramped during testing, about 71% of football data came from off-season conditioning, and the authors note possible type II errors; the sixfold odds figure for sweat rate per body surface area comes from a variable whose AUC was not significant (Table 5).
paper.practicalImplications: Heavy-sweating American football players may benefit from individual sweat-rate monitoring, with electrolyte or fluid replacement considered for them. For most athletes, the study does not support routine fluid or electrolyte loading to prevent cramps, because over-drinking carries a risk of hyponatremia.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the study suggests sweat rate and sweat electrolyte losses vary widely by sex and sport, so hydration plans should be individualized rather than one size fits all. It does not test whether fluid or electrolyte interventions improve performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the study does not address return to sport after injury, because athletes were excluded if they had injuries and none cramped during testing. It cannot be used to guide cramp management during return to play.

records.sourceFile: Swifter higher stronger - What's on the menu.pdf

paper.citation: Burke LM, Hawley JA. Swifter, higher, stronger: What's on the menu? Science. 2018;362(6416):781-787.
paper.abstract: This review examines the nutritional approaches used to support elite athletic performance, including fuel use, periodized training nutrition, competition fueling and supplements. The authors argue that sports nutrition should reflect the specific demands of each sport and the periodization of training rather than a single athletic diet.
paper.tldr: Sports nutrition should be matched to the demands of each sport and each training session, not a single athletic diet. Carbohydrate availability, periodized train-low sessions and a small set of supplements with good evidence form the core of the approach.
paper.methods: A narrative review in Science, with no described systematic search or inclusion criteria. The authors discuss published research and examples from elite athletes, including their own work, and frame the evidence with a hierarchy of study designs.
paper.findings: Carbohydrate is the main fuel for most sports, and daily carbohydrate intake typically varies from about 2 to 12 g per kg body mass across training cycles. Train-low sessions augment cellular responses, but translation to performance has been less clear: early studies failed to detect superior performance, while better integration of train-low and train-high sessions has been linked to superior performance in subelite populations. Competition guidance cites carbohydrate intakes of 30-60 g per hour for events up to 2-3 hours and 60-90 g per hour for ultra-endurance events. The review notes that few supplements have robust evidence, citing caffeine, creatine, bicarbonate, beta-alanine and nitrate, and that some interventions, such as beetroot juice, appear less effective in elite competitors.
paper.limitations: As a narrative review, the article does not use a systematic search, so evidence selection cannot be verified. The authors state that most research participants are sub-elite, often male, and that studies with elite athletes are underpowered or rare. The authors receive funding and honoraria from sports nutrition and food industry partners, which they disclose.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can match carbohydrate, protein and fluid plans to the demands of each session and event rather than applying one diet. Train-low sessions are best treated as a targeted tool within a periodized plan, because their translation to performance has been less clear than their effect on cellular responses.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review supports periodizing carbohydrate and protein around training sessions and planning event fueling, including gut training and mouth rinsing. It also notes that many supplements lack robust evidence and that the performance benefit of train-low strategies is less clear than their cellular effects.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review does not address injury rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot be used to guide return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: The 4R's framework of nutritional strategies for post-exercise recovery - A review with emphasis on new generation of carbohydrates.pdf

paper.citation: Bonilla DA, Pérez-Idárraga A, Odriozola-Martínez A, Kreider RB. The 4R's Framework of Nutritional Strategies for Post-Exercise Recovery: A Review with Emphasis on New Generation of Carbohydrates. Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health. 2021;18:103.
paper.abstract: The review summarises nutritional strategies for post-exercise recovery and proposes a 4R framework (Rehydrate, Refuel, Repair, Rest). It discusses new carbohydrate formulations, which the authors say need further research.
paper.tldr: Nutrition after training can be organised as four steps: rehydrate, refuel, repair and rest. The authors favour carbohydrate plus protein for refuelling and cite creatine and pre-sleep casein as helpful, but they also note that adding protein does not raise glycogen synthesis when carbohydrate intake is sufficient, and newer bioengineered carbohydrates still need more research.
paper.methods: Review using a database search of ScienceDirect, PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar with the string 'nutrition AND (exercise recovery OR sports recovery)', plus hand-searching, which returned 1816 records screened by article type, text availability and suitability. English papers from 2010 onward were prioritised, and papers not analysing recovery, abstracts without full text, and studies of performance- and image-enhancing drugs were excluded.
paper.findings: The authors recommend at least 150% of body weight lost to be replaced after exercise, with sodium if faster replacement is needed. For refuelling, they describe carbohydrate and protein together as a good strategy to replenish glycogen while supporting repair, at multiple intervals after exercise. For repair, they cite high-quality protein and creatine monohydrate, with tart cherry, beetroot juice and possibly ashwagandha as possible aids. For rest, they cite pre-sleep casein as effective for muscle adaptation during resistance training, with more research needed in endurance athletes. No pooled effect sizes are reported.
paper.limitations: Screening criteria are loose (article type, text availability, suitability), and no risk-of-bias appraisal or sample-level results are reported. Several recommendations are drawn from studies the authors describe as heterogeneous, and the evidence for newer carbohydrates and for endurance athletes is limited. Two authors declare ties to supplement companies, including the Creapure creatine advisory board.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the 4R framework as a structure for post-training nutrition planning, adjusting fluid, carbohydrate, protein and sleep choices to the sport, the time to the next session and the athlete. Do not apply the specific rehydration volume or supplement suggestions as fixed prescriptions, since the authors present them as a strategic framework.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Use the framework to plan recovery nutrition between sessions, with carbohydrate and protein at multiple intervals and fluid and sodium replacement matched to sweat losses. The paper gives no evidence on performance outcomes from these strategies.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper is not designed for return to sport. It can inform general nutrition for recovery after training load increases, but it gives no criteria for returning from injury and does not address injured athletes.

records.sourceFile: The 4Rs Framework of Sports Nutrition - An Update with Recommendations to Evaluate Allostatic Load in Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Bonilla DA, Stout JR, Gleeson M, Campbell BI, Escalante G, Rojas-Valverde D, et al. The 4Rs Framework of Sports Nutrition: An Update with Recommendations to Evaluate Allostatic Load in Athletes. Life. 2025;15:867.
paper.abstract: The paper updates the 4Rs sports nutrition framework for post-exercise recovery within the allostasis model. It offers practical recommendations for assessing allostatic load in athletes and proposes a cautious allostatic load index for physique competitors and elite athletes.
paper.tldr: The 4Rs (Rehydrate, Refuel, Repair, Recuperate) remain a practical recovery framework, and the paper adds a proposed biomarker index to track cumulative physiological stress in elite and physique athletes. The index is a starting point that still needs validation before use in decisions.
paper.methods: Review incorporating PRISMA-ScR elements, with searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science and Google Scholar using free-text terms on sports nutrition, allostasis and allostatic load, plus a biomarker database and manual reference-list searching. Results are presented in narrative form.
paper.findings: The authors recommend replacing at least 150% of body mass lost, with sodium if faster replacement is needed. They cite about 1.2 g/kg per hour of carbohydrate for up to 4 hours after exercise for refuelling, and state that a ketogenic diet generally has neutral or negative effects on athletic performance compared with carbohydrate-rich diets. Creatine monohydrate may help recovery, while tart cherry, omega-3 fatty acids and dietary nitrate need further clinical research. The proposed ALindex sums 10 equally weighted biomarkers, each scored 0 or 1 against a cut-off, giving a 0 to 10 index; it is proposed but not tested in this paper.
paper.limitations: The information is primarily associative, with little multilevel, causal or complexity-based analysis. The proposed biomarker set needs validation, and the authors note that sex-specific cut-offs and individual monitoring may be warranted for elite athletes. Blood draws must be standardised (rested, fasted, not after high-intensity work) for the index to be reliable. Several authors declare supplement-industry ties, including membership of a Creapure-sponsored creatine advisory board.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the 4Rs as a structure for post-training nutrition, with carbohydrate and protein refuelling matched to the time to the next session. Treat the ALindex as an exploratory way to organise biomarker data for physique and elite athletes, and validate its cut-offs locally before using it to change training or nutrition.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The framework supports post-exercise nutrition planning, and the ALindex may help organise biomarker and load data to spot cumulative stress in elite and physique athletes. The paper does not show that using the index improves performance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper addresses recovery nutrition and allostatic load in athletes, and the authors mention injury recovery as part of the Recuperate step. It provides no return-to-sport criteria and no evidence on returning from injury.

records.sourceFile: The Efficacy of Nutritional Strategies and Ergogenic Aids on Acute Responses and Chronic Adaptations to Exertional-Heat Exposure - A Narrative Review.pdf

paper.citation: Dunn RA, Tinsley GM, Palmer TB, Benjamin CL, Sekiguchi Y. The Efficacy of Nutritional Strategies and Ergogenic Aids on Acute Responses and Chronic Adaptations to Exertional-Heat Exposure: A Narrative Review. Nutrients. 2024;16:3792.
paper.abstract: Review of nutritional strategies and ergogenic aids (hydration, sodium, carbohydrate, protein, caffeine, nitrate, tyrosine and creatine) for acute exertional heat exposure and heat acclimation. The authors find robust evidence for some aids and equivocal findings for others, which depend on test type, duration, outcome and sex.
paper.tldr: In this review, sodium before exercise in the heat, carbohydrate during prolonged sessions and creatine have the most support, while caffeine and carbohydrate-plus-protein results are mixed and nitrate and tyrosine showed no consistent benefit in heat. Treat the doses as starting points, since the underlying trials vary widely.
paper.methods: Narrative review with a predetermined search of PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Google Scholar through April 2024, for studies in human participants with ambient temperature above 28 C and, where relevant, heat acclimation of at least 5 days. Trial results are summarized in tables, but no formal risk-of-bias tool or pooled analysis is used.
paper.findings: Sodium loading of 20 to 40 mg/kg 1 to 2 hours before exercise improved plasma volume and thermoregulation in some trials, and creatine did not impair thermoregulation and improved performance in some. Caffeine often raised core temperature, nitrate did not improve performance or thermoregulation in heat, and tyrosine results were mixed. Carbohydrate of 30 to 90 g per hour was recommended for prolonged exercise, and added protein showed no performance advantage when carbohydrate delivery was 60 g per hour or more.
paper.limitations: There is no formal quality assessment, and the authors acknowledge selection bias, so the recommendations rest partly on judgment. Many trials are small, and the authors say sex-specific and modality-specific responses are unclear, which limits prescription for particular groups. The review concerns exercise in the heat in general, not injured athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest sodium before exercise in the heat, carbohydrate at about 30 to 90 g per hour in prolonged sessions (toward the upper end for males), and added protein for recovery, which may help. They advise caution with caffeine because it can raise core temperature, and they note that nitrate and tyrosine have weak support in heat.
paper.athleteDev: For performance in the heat, the review points to sodium before exercise and enough carbohydrate during long sessions as the most practical starting points. Caffeine can raise core temperature, and nitrate and tyrosine are not supported as reliable heat-performance aids in this review.
paper.rtp: The review covers acute and chronic heat exposure in general exercise rather than injured athletes or recovery from injury, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.
